paper.title: Consumption Network Effects
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement appears in the article; the data are Danish administrative tax records matched with IDA and the Danish Expenditure Survey, and no Statistics Denmark project number is given.

registers.name_in_paper: administrative longitudinal tax records for the Danish population
variables_mentioned: implicit tax on the consumption value of owned housing TH
assets A (cash, bank deposits, stocks and shares, property value, cars and other vehicles, minus liabilities)

registers.name_in_paper: Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: linkage and sample frame: identifies co-workers (peer groups) and supplies demographics, occupation, education and firm/plant characteristics used as controls and instruments
variables_mentioned: occupation group (blue collar, white collar, manager)
firm legal type (publicly traded, limited liability, other)

registers.role: outcomes for the mechanism tests: budget shares by good category and a survey-based consumption measure

linkages: Tax records matched with IDA employer-employee data to identify co-workers (same plant; for public employees the physical address of the workplace)
Spouses linked into households; couples where both spouses work and do not work in the same plant
Distance-1 peers = co-workers; distance-2 peers = spouses of co-workers; distance-3 peers = co-workers of the spouses of co-workers
Danish Expenditure Survey households (1994-1996) matched with the tax records, giving the 'ALL' sample and, for households also satisfying the baseline restrictions, the 'MATCH' sample

sample.universe: Danish households in the administrative tax records, 1980-1996
selection_rules: Both spouses work and are employees rather than self-employed
Households are dropped once one or both members stop working or become self-employed
Couples who work in the same plant are excluded
Cases creating feedback network effects (two couples whose members work in the same two firms) are discarded when constructing instruments
Peers' consumption is computed over all workers, including singles and households with only one spouse working
Table A1 in the online Appendix details the step-by-step selection process; most observations are lost when focusing on working, married individuals whose spouse also works
sample.n_observations: 2,671,889 household-year observations in the baseline estimation sample

construction_notes: Consumption is imputed from the dynamic budget constraint: C_it = Y_it - T_it - Delta A_it, with Y = GY + HS + CS - TH (equation 1)
All monetary values are in 2000 DKr prices (1$ = 7.33 DKr)
Consumption is expressed per adult equivalent using the Luxembourg Income Study scale, sqrt(n_it) where n_it is family size
All regression variables are expressed in first differences
Peers are weighted by omega_(is,jm) = (d_(is,jm) + 1)^-2, where d is the sum of the absolute differences in education group (5 groups) and occupation group (3 groups)

Alternative weighting schemes used in robustness: linear, extended quadratic including two age ranges (40 and less, more than 40), and a sharp scheme treating all same-plant same-occupation workers equally
Goods are classified as visible, neutral (food at home only) or not visible using the Heffetz (2011) visibility index; a 30-category disaggregation reproduces Heffetz's categories except charity
Tenure is measured as years with the current employer within the 1980-1996 window and is left-censored
Standard errors are double clustered for husbands and wives at the workplace, occupation and education level
Less than 5% of households ever change spousal composition, so divorce and separation are abstracted from

claims.statement: In an OLS first-difference Euler equation, a higher growth rate of the wife's co-workers' average consumption is associated with higher household consumption growth.

treatment.label: Wife's peers' average log consumption, first difference (Delta ln C-bar^w_it)

register_source.value: Danish administrative longitudinal tax records (income and assets); the paper names no register variable codes; peer groups formed from Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA), employer-employee data: firm and plant IDs, occupation, education

definition.value: Weighted average of the log consumption of a spouse's co-workers (individuals working in the same plant), weighted by the quadratic weight omega = (d+1)^-2 where d is the 'degree of separation' in education and occupation groups; entered in first differences. Peer consumption is computed over all workers, including singles and households with only one spouse working.

timing.value: Annual first difference, same year t as the outcome

outcome.label: Log of adult equivalent household consumption, first difference (Delta ln C_it)

register_source.value: Danish administrative longitudinal tax records (income and assets); the paper names no register variable codes

definition.value: Total household consumption (spending) imputed from the dynamic budget constraint, C_it = Y_it - T_it - Delta A_it, where Y is gross income plus housing support plus child support minus the implicit tax on owned housing, T total tax payments and Delta A the change in asset values; expressed per adult equivalent using the LIS scale sqrt(n_it), in 2000 DKr, in logs and first-differenced.

timing.value: Annual; year-t minus year-(t-1) change, contemporaneous with the peer-consumption change

units.value: elasticity: log points of household adult-equivalent consumption per log point of peers' average consumption (both in first differences)

estimand.target_population: Danish dual-earner employee couples with a head aged 18-65 observed in the tax registers 1980-1996
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous annual response: the first difference of consumption in year t is related to the first difference of peers' consumption in the same year

population.description: Danish households whose head is aged 18-65 in which both spouses work as employees (not self-employed) and do not work in the same plant, 1980-1996
subgroups_defined: By network size, age, years of schooling, share of women peers, GDP growth rate
population.selection: Households are included only while both spouses work as employees; they leave the sample once one or both stop working or become self-employed. Couples working in the same plant are excluded. Table A1 of the online Appendix details the step-by-step selection.

identification.source_of_variation: None exogenous: cross-household variation in peers' consumption growth after first differencing and conditioning on a rich set of controls

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability of peers' consumption growth given first differencing and the full set of individual, household and contextual controls plus year dummies.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not supported: Durbin-Hausman-Wu exogeneity tests reported in Table 4 reject the null of exogeneity (p = 0.002 and 0.015 for separate networks; 0.001 and 0.004 for the joint network).

rhs: Unobserved determinants of household log consumption growth

implies_edges.from: Individual, household and contextual controls (incl. own-firm variables and year dummies)

key_assumptions.assumption: Peers' consumption is measured without error; the authors state the opposite and argue measurement error biases OLS downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.2 argues OLS is attenuated by measurement error in peers' consumption, exacerbated by first differencing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the estimation sample: only dual-earner couples of employees (head aged 18-65).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.1 and Table A1 of the online Appendix.

implies_edges.from: Dual-earner employee couple, head aged 18-65 (sample inclusion)

threats_discussed: Reflection problem / simultaneity of own and peers' consumption (Manski 1993)
Contextual effects: co-workers share traits that determine consumption
Correlated effects: common unobserved firm-level shocks to all workers in a plant
Measurement error in the register-based consumption measure (capital gains and losses)
Measurement error in the definition of the peer group
Sorting of workers into firms on permanent income or on preferences
Endogenous mobility across plants
Feedback network effects between two firms linked by two couples
robustness_checks: Plant stayers only (Table 5, column 2)
Firm-to-firm transition fixed effects (Table 5, column 3)
Region-year dummies for local shocks (Table 5, column 4)
Sector-year dummies for sector shocks (Table 5, column 5)
Trimming top and bottom 1% of the consumption distribution (Table 6, column 2)
Excluding stockholders (Table 6, column 3)
Renters only (Table 6, column 4)
Alternative peer weighting schemes: linear, extended quadratic with age, sharp same-occupation (Table 6, columns 5-7)
Placebo scrambled firm assignment, 50 replications (Table 6, column 8)
Plants with no change in workforce composition (online Appendix Table A2, column 2)
Adding spouses' age and education in levels (online Appendix Table A2, column 3)
Durbin-Hausman-Wu test for sorting on preferences, double-differenced estimator (footnote 13, p-value 12%)
unresolved_confounders: Endogenous mobility across plants: 'we do not have powerful exclusion restrictions to perform this exercise' (footnote 14)
Imperfect measurement of the true social network: some co-workers exert no social influence and some non-co-workers do
Low power of the instruments once the sample is sliced by interactive effects (heterogeneity analysis)
Lower power of the intratemporal (demand) test than of the intertemporal (Euler equation) test

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic firm-level variation (firm size, firm employment growth, firm legal type, public-sector status) at the workplaces of distance-3 peers - the co-workers of the spouses of one's own co-workers - combined with the intransitive-triad structure created by spouses working in different plants, Denmark 1980-1996.
identification.instrument: Weighted averages of distance-3 peers' firm-specific variables ('Firm IV's': firm size, firm-specific change in employment, firm type dummies, public sector dummy) and, in some columns, weighted averages of distance-3 peers' demographics ('Demographic IV's': age, age squared, years of schooling, share of women, shares by occupation, # kids 0-6, # kids 7-13), all in first differences.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the firm-level variables (and demographics) of distance-3 peers affect the household's own consumption growth only indirectly, through the consumption of its own peers, and not directly.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Economic argument in Section 4.1.1 and footnote 12; overidentification tests reported in Table 4 (p-value 0.216 in column 3, 0.280 in column 6); the placebo scrambled-firm exercise in Table 6 column (8).

implies_edges.from: Distance-3 peers' firm-level variables (firm size, firm employment growth, firm type, public sector)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: distance-3 peers' firm-level variables move the average consumption of the household's own peers.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage F-statistics reported in Table 4 (78.27 wife, 59.85 husband in column 3; 111.40 in column 6) and in Tables 5 and 6.

implies_edges.from: Distance-3 peers' firm-level variables (firm size, firm employment growth, firm type, public sector)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional exogeneity of the instruments: given own-firm variables, year dummies and the full set of individual, household and contextual controls, the distance-3 instruments are independent of the unobserved determinants of household consumption growth (no residual correlated effects).
key_assumptions.supported_by: First differencing removes household and firm fixed effects; robustness to plant stayers and firm-to-firm transition fixed effects (Table 5, columns 2-3) and to region-year and sector-year dummies (Table 5, columns 4-5).

rhs: Unobserved determinants of household log consumption growth

implies_edges.from: Individual, household and contextual controls (incl. own-firm variables and year dummies)

key_assumptions.assumption: Plant-specific effects may remain in the error term after first differencing and generate correlated effects (an unobserved common cause of own and peers' consumption growth) - conceded by the authors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.1.1; addressed by restricting to plant stayers and by adding firm-to-firm transition fixed effects (Table 5).

implies_edges.from: Unobserved plant-level shocks

key_assumptions.assumption: No feedback network effects: pairs of firms that are mutually connected through spouses (so that the household's own shocks would enter its own instrument) are discarded when the instruments are built.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.1.2 states the cases are discarded; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the estimation sample: only dual-earner couples of employees (head aged 18-65) who do not work in the same plant are used, and households leave the sample once a spouse stops working or becomes self-employed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.1 and Table A1 of the online Appendix; the authors state the selection is driven by the research design, not by outcomes.

implies_edges.from: Dual-earner employee couple, head aged 18-65 (sample inclusion)

key_assumptions.assumption: Measured co-worker networks approximate the true reference group; networks may be measured with error (some co-workers exert no influence, some non-co-workers do).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4; the authors argue the IV strategy corrects for this classical measurement error (footnote 19).

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic firm-level variation (firm size, firm employment growth, firm legal type, public-sector status) at the workplaces of distance-3 peers - the co-workers of the spouses of one's own co-workers - combined with the intransitive-triad structure created by spouses working in different plants, Denmark 1980-1996.
identification.instrument: Weighted averages of distance-3 peers' firm-specific variables ('Firm IV's': firm size, firm-specific change in employment, firm type dummies, public sector dummy) and, in some columns, weighted averages of distance-3 peers' demographics ('Demographic IV's': age, age squared, years of schooling, share of women, shares by occupation, # kids 0-6, # kids 7-13), all in first differences.
